content:
I have two related issues and I would like some advice on if/how it should be fixed:

(1) A LinearOrder Prop instance docs#Prop.linearOrder is defined in mathlib without scoping under Classical. As a result, because of docs#LinearOrder.toDecidableEq, we have DecidableEq Prop synthesizable without opening Classical. Informally, this is tantamount to saying that every Prop is decidable (because we have ∀ p, Decidable (p = True)).

We can define the following function without opening Classical. Although it is not idiomatic (it should be if p then 1 else 0), it can occur as an instantiation of a larger definition (e.g., counting True in a Multiset Prop).

import Mathlib
noncomputable def a (p : Prop) := if p = True then 1 else 0

(2) Regardless of whether it is scoped under Classical, this creates an instance diamond:

import Mathlib

-- I have a definition `a`
noncomputable def a (p : Prop) := if p = True then 1 else 0

-- suppose in a `classical` proof, or in a separate definition, I have
open Classical in
noncomputable def b (p : Prop) := if p = True then 1 else 0

example (p : Prop) : a p = b p := rfl  --fails

a and b are not definitionally equal because the first uses LinearOrder.toDecidableEq and the DecidableEq Prop instance is just Classical.propDecidable, while the second uses instDecidableEqOfIff on instDecidableIff with a non-Classical instDecidableTrue. (See Mathlib/RingTheory/Norm/Transitivity.lean for a real-world example).

My questions are:

  • Is this an issue to be fixed?
  • Should we make the instance scoped under Classical? Note that doing this works with open scoped Classical in ... but might not work with the classical tactic, in that writing classical might not make LinearOrder Prop available, because classical only adds docs#Classical.propDecidable which alone does not infer LinearOrder Prop because docs#Lattice.toLinearOrder is a non-instance.

Hello! I happened upon this issue and I'd like to revive this thread.
This seems weird:

import Mathlib
#synth DecidableEq Prop

As explained above, this is because of the noncomputable LinearOrder instance on Prop. I know some want to separate out the decidability from LinearOrder in the future, but for now we could avoid the issue for Prop.

Turning the LinearOrder & CompleteLinearOrder instances into defs and fixing whatever breaks is only a +22/-9 change.

Reals also have a noncomputable DecidableEq instance, but that's intended to avoid spamming theorems with DecidableEq ℝ or open Classical. However for Props it feels less natural, LinearOrder is less useful, the change is small, and also note that we have docs#instDecidableEqOfIff (instance [Decidable (p ↔ q)] → Decidable (p = q)) which causes diamonds with the DecidableEq Prop instance, unlike for ℝ.

Thoughts?

Snir Broshi said:

Reals also have a noncomputable DecidableEq instance, but that's intended to avoid spamming theorems with DecidableEq ℝ or open Classical.

I think the argument here is rather "We know that no computable instance for DecidableEq ℝ can possibly exist, and so there is no harm caused in providing a noncomputable one"
Perhaps the harm you are perceiving here could be resolved by #synth also indicating whether the instance is computable?
I'd love that regardless, but what do you suggest doing about the existing diamonds?
Other than the diamonds, I'm mostly worried that code using ite/dite can accidentally introduce classical logic to a def when the author meant to use some Decidable instance

I like the idea of "put classical decidable instances on objects which cannot get non-classical ones" -- we put classical decidable equality on the p-adic numbers in FLT for example. Isn't the thing to do, to remove the decidable equality stuff in LinearOrder, like how we removed it from Field many years ago? Although I have forgotten why it's there in the first place and there is no doubt an annoyingly good reason.

Kevin Buzzard said:

I like the idea of "put classical decidable instances on objects which cannot get non-classical ones"

Does this extend to Prop? It isn't like other objects, for example it is used in ifs and Decidable itself, and equality of two Props is also a Prop. So it's in a unique position.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Isn't the thing to do, to remove the decidable equality stuff in LinearOrder

Yeah, but does this mean you agree with removing DecidableEq Prop?
(AFAICT it only exists because there was a nice LinearOrder Prop, and DecidableEq came along for the ride when linear_order merged with decidable_linear_order).

Because if so, then instead of waiting for a big refactor (AFAIK no one is working on it, and it's difficult), we should fix it now with the +22/-9 change. The LinearOrder thing is mostly independent from the question of whether we should have DecidableEq Prop.

I know exactly why one would want a classical decidable equality on the reals (because it makes code cleaner, and putting one on the p-adics made FLT cleaner) but I am unclear about why one would want one on Prop so I am not sure I can give a useful opinion.

Opened #42369
Also added a test to make sure that #synth DecidableEq Prop fails.
I checked git blame on LinearOrder and it seems it was PR #18 that merged lean3's linear_order and decidable_linear_order into a single LinearOrder

In #42577, I tried removing the DecidableEq and DecidableLT fields. However, doing so would require either introducing local Decidable instances in some definitions or adding extra Decidable instance parameters wherever those definitions are used.

Another option would be to make greater use of Ord and compare, which might also make it possible to remove DecidableLE. Would that make sense for mathlib?
I think it would be very weird for LinearOrder to bundle compare but not DecidableEq
